How do I start my action in the Superior Court?

Where things stand

Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.

What to do next

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

What happens after

The registrar issues your document by dating, signing and sealing it with the court's seal and giving it a court file number. You must serve a statement of claim within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve both together within six months after the notice of action is issued.

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

How do I start my action in the Superior Court?

Where things stand

Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.

What to do next

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

How do I start my action in the Superior Court?

Where things stand

Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.

What to do next

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

The Limitations Act presumes you knew about your claim on the day it happened, unless you can prove you learned of it later. So this is counted from the date you gave for when it happened.

The registrar issues your document by dating, signing and sealing it with the court's seal and giving it a court file number. You must serve a statement of claim within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve both together within six months after the notice of action is issued.

How do I start my action in the Superior Court?

Where things stand

Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.

What to do next

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

The Limitations Act presumes you knew about your claim on the day it happened, unless you can prove you learned of it later. So this is counted from the date you gave for when it happened.

Waksdale v. Swegon North America Inc., 2020 ONCA 391, paras. 7-8

“Termination clauses should be interpreted in a way that encourages employers to draft agreements that comply with the ESA.”

A court decision: what the judges said in an earlier case. It has not been checked for later decisions that may have changed it.

Read more of the decision

[7] The law regarding the interpretation of termination clauses in employment contracts was helpfully summarized by Laskin J.A. at para. 28 of Wood v. Fred Deeley Imports Ltd., 2017 ONCA 158, 134 O.R. (3d) 481. The following points from that summary are particularly apt for the purposes of this appeal: • The ESA is remedial legislation, intended to protect the interests of employees. Courts should thus favour an interpretation of the ESA that “encourages employers to comply with the minimum requirements of the Act” and “extends its protections to as many employees as possible”, over an interpretation that does not do so: Machtinger, p. 1003. • Termination clauses should be interpreted in a way that encourages employers to draft agreements that comply with the ESA. If the only consequence employers suffer for drafting a termination clause that fails to comply with the ESA is an order that they comply, then they will have little or no incentive to draft a lawful termination clause at the beginning of the employment relationship: Machtinger, p. 1004. [8] Laskin J.A. went on to observe that the enforceability of a termination provision in an employment contract must be determined as at the time the agreement was executed. The wording of the contract alone should be considered in deciding whether it contravenes the ESA, not what the employer might have done on termination: Wood, at paras, 43-44. Thus, even if an employer’s actions comply with its ESA obligations on termination, that compliance does not have the effect of saving a termination provision that violates the ESA.

Read more of the decision

[157] A wrongfully dismissed employee has a duty to try to mitigate her damages by making reasonable best efforts to obtain a position that is reasonably comparable in salary and responsibility to the one from which she was wrongfully dismissed. If she is able to secure such a position, her earnings are deducted from her damages as mitigation.4 If she turns down such a position, or fails to make reasonable best efforts, then the amount she could have earned at a comparable position is similarly deducted from her damages, based on a failure to meet the duty to mitigate. But if she can only find a position that is not comparable in either salary or responsibility, she is entitled to turn it down, and if she does, the amount she could have earned is not deducted from her damages. [158] It follows, in my view, that where a wrongfully dismissed employee is effectively forced to accept a much inferior position because no comparable position is available, the amount she earns in that position is not mitigation of damages and need not be deducted from the amount the employer must pay.

The general deadline to start a court case. Based on the date you gave us, the last day for this is Friday 30 June 2028.

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

How do I start my action in the Superior Court?

Where things stand

Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.

What to do next

The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

Fred Deeley Imports Ltd., 2017 ONCA 158, 134 O.R. (3d) 481. The wording of the contract alone should be considered in deciding whether it contravenes the ESA, not what the employer might have done on termination: Wood, at paras, 43-44. Thus, even if an employer’s actions comply with its ESA obligations on termination, that compliance does not have the effect of saving a termination provision that violates the ESA.
